A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SAN and retain identifiable method and experiment counterparts. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–G, which were also inspected.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification experiments in Table 1, comparisons across three backbones in Figure 2, and a component ablation in Figure 3.

after.justification: v2 reports vision experiments, LLaMA commonsense-reasoning and LLaVA visual-language results, additional ablations, and robotic video-generation examples in Appendix G.

M1.justification: v2 extends the original SSF-style scaling procedure with a pooled adjusted/original-output ratio for LoRA integration and propagation to corresponding layers in subsequent blocks (Section 3.2 and Appendix C). It also integrates SAN with DoRA. v1's explicitly described learned affine recalibration step, Eqs. 12–13, disappears from the method description.

E1.justification: The visual benchmark coverage is retained despite v2's inconsistent abstract count. v2 adds eight commonsense-reasoning datasets, seven visual-language benchmarks, and RoboVQA-based robotic video prediction using DynamiCrafter in Appendix G. These introduce substantially different domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: The main vision comparison adds NOAH, AdaptFormer and SPT-LoRA; new language comparisons include DoRA, P-Tuning v2, series/parallel adapters and ChatGPT with chain-of-thought. Conversely, the backbone radar drops Bitfit, LoRA, Adapter and VPT, retaining FFT, LP, SSF and SAN. Appendix Table 7 drops the earlier detailed Adapter results, although aggregate Adapter comparisons remain in Table 1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces multiple 7–13B language-model configurations, three-epoch language and one-epoch visual-language training, paired rank-8/16 vision settings, and rank-16/32 language controls. Appendix G introduces four criteria for evaluating generated robotic actions. The retained vision schedule remains 100 epochs with 10 warm-up epochs; newly disclosed vision hyperparameters alone do not establish changed experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds ordered-versus-random propagation tests, applied-layer and learning-rate comparisons, rank sensitivity, cross-layer distribution analyses, and robotic-generation case studies (Figure 5 and Appendices B–G). v1's dedicated component-separation ablation, including propagation-only results in Figure 3, is removed. The analysis now addresses substantially broader questions about propagation and compatibility.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's scaling-vector means, variances and histograms characterize learned parameter distributions rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial language, visual-language, ablation and video-generation results. Existing vision values also change: SAN's general CIFAR-100/ImageNet-1k accuracies move from 94.11/83.69 to 94.2/83.8. The reported VTAB mean changes from 75.00 to 77.7 despite largely retained per-dataset scores in Appendix Table 7, so this summary change does not establish a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for pooled LoRA-derived scales and blockwise propagation, while removing v1's affine-recalibration equations. The central linear reparameterization and quadratic regularization arguments remain substantially unchanged. No new theorem or formal proof is supplied.

C1.justification: v1 presents SAN primarily as a biologically inspired PEFT method validated on vision tasks. v2 claims a general plug-and-play enhancement for existing PEFT methods across scalable vision, language and multimodal models, and elevates neural-engram-like task-specific adjustment patterns to a main contribution. This substantially broadens the claimed contribution and applicability.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting within-task similarity and between-task differences to neural engrams, random-propagation failures to layer proximity, and rank robustness to simplified adjustment requirements. Optimization-stability reasoning replaces v1's affine compensation rationale for nonlinearities. Some new interpretation overstates the evidence: Section 4.3 attributes 2.4–4.6-point gains to comparison with DoRA, whereas Table 2 shows those gains against LoRA.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B add dataset-specific learning rates and drop-path rates, model-specific batch sizes, search procedures, SSF/DoRA code-base pointers, and training hardware and budgets for new tasks. v1 provides mainly an optimizer, schedule and GPU description. v2 also revises the vision hardware description from RTX 3090 to RTX 3090 Ti. Its own code and W&B logs remain promised rather than released within the PDF.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions SAN around neural engrams and compatibility with LoRA/DoRA, adding related discussion of DoRA, limitations of LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and engram research. It expands language, multimodal and video-model references while reducing the earlier detailed heterosynaptic-plasticity discussion. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are substantially rewritten, including an explicit contribution list. Method explanations are reordered, and experiments are reorganized around vision, language and visual-language tasks. The new appendix structure separates configurations, variants, analyses and detailed results.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, replaces the original composite schematic with redesigned pipeline and propagation diagrams, and redraws the backbone radar. The detailed vision table is reorganized into a main summary and Appendix Table 7. New tables, distribution plots, a heatmap, ablation charts and video-generation panels substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v1's portability and mechanism claims had limited empirical support and sparse implementation detail. v2 directly tests integration with LoRA/DoRA on large language and visual-language models, probes rank and propagation choices, and supplies dataset- and model-specific configurations. These substantially strengthen validation and reproducibility. Losing the original component ablation and retaining numerical/comparator inconsistencies, notably Table 1 versus Table 7 and Section 4.3 versus Table 2, limit confidence but do not outweigh those gains.
